To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the implication and realizability problems for MSCs are decidable and that the synthesis problem is polynomial-time reducible to the implication problem.

(1) MSC implication is decidable and polynomial-time solvable; (2) MSC realizability is decidable and, for the safe case, polynomial-time solvable, while the general case is NP-complete; (3) MSC synthesis can be solved in polynomial time.
(i) the implication problem is decidable and in NP, and (ii) realizability and synthesis are decidable and in PSPACE
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of inferring the set of behaviors that is "implied" (or "realized") by a set of MSCs, and the problem of synthesizing state machines realizing the set of MSCs.
the formal analysis of message sequence charts and the development of algorithms for checking the realizability, synthesis, and implication of message sequence charts.
the formalization and automatic analysis of the informal process of drawing MSCs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our framework provides a sound and complete basis for the analysis of Message Sequence Charts, and that it provides a solid basis for the synthesis of concurrent state machines realizing given MSCs.

, given an MSC specification S, the following can be computed in polynomial time: (1) a set of all MSCs that are implied by S; (2) a set of MSCs that can be realized by a concurrent state machine that implements S; (3) a concurrent state machine realizing S; (4) a concurrent state-machine implementation of S that is deadlock-free.

, given a set of MSCs, we can decide whether they are safe, we can decide if they are safe-realizable (and, if so, we can synthesize an implementation), and if they are unsafe, we can derive a set of implied MSCs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have provided a complete solution for the problem of inferring message sequence charts.
we provide a framework for the formal analysis of Message Sequence Charts.

, given a finite set of MSCs, one can check in polynomial time whether the given MSCs are safe, whether the given MSC set is realizable, and, if so, one can synthesize an implementation of the given MSCs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the formal framework we propose can be used to automatically analyze and synthesize Message Sequence Charts, thus providing a useful tool to software designers.
the MSC formalism is a powerful tool for the early modeling and analysis of concurrent systems.
, in the presence of a finite set of MSCs, one can automatically derive all the MSCs that are realizable by a concurrent system.
